metadata.author: Greg Paskal
metadata.description: Referrer-Policy header missing finding template with comprehensive guidance for all audiences including framework-specific implementation code, server configurations, and testing strategies to prevent sensitive information leakage through HTTP Referer headers when users navigate from one site to another or from HTTPS to HTTP pages.

EXECUTIVE.summary: Your application lacks Referrer-Policy protection, potentially leaking sensitive information in URLs (session tokens, user IDs, search queries) to external third-party sites when users click outbound links.
EXECUTIVE.businessRisk: Low to medium risk of privacy violations and sensitive data exposure through URL referrer leakage. When users click links to external sites, the full URL (including query parameters) may be sent in the HTTP Referer header, potentially exposing: session tokens, authentication parameters, user IDs, search queries, internal file paths, API keys in URLs. Privacy-focused industries (healthcare, finance, legal) face elevated compliance risk. GDPR Article 25 requires data protection by design. Minimal direct financial impact but can damage user trust and brand reputation if sensitive data leaks.
EXECUTIVE.complianceImpact: GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design) recommends minimizing data exposure. ISO 27001 information security controls. OWASP Privacy Best Practices. Some regional privacy laws (CCPA, PIPEDA) may require referrer control. Generally low compliance priority but considered best practice for privacy-conscious organizations.

PROJECT_MANAGER.summary: Missing Referrer-Policy header allows full URL information (including sensitive parameters) to leak to external sites when users click outbound links. Simple one-line fix with minimal risk.
PROJECT_MANAGER.timeline: Can be addressed in current or next sprint. Implementation takes 30 minutes to 1 hour including testing. Very low complexity change. Low priority unless application handles sensitive data in URLs or operates in privacy-sensitive industry (healthcare, finance).
PROJECT_MANAGER.effort: 30 minutes to 1 hour for implementation and testing. Zero-risk change with no functional impact on core features.
dependencies: Access to web server or application configuration
Understanding of application's URL structure and external links

DEVELOPER.summary: Referrer-Policy HTTP response header is not present, allowing browsers to send full URL information (including sensitive query parameters) in the Referer header when users navigate to external sites.
DEVELOPER.technical: Referrer-Policy is an HTTP response header that controls how much referrer information browsers include when navigating away from a page. Without this header, browsers use default behavior (often 'no-referrer-when-downgrade') which sends full URL to same-protocol destinations. Sensitive data in URLs can leak: session tokens (?token=abc123), user IDs (?user_id=12345), search queries (?q=sensitive+search), API keys, internal paths. Policy values: 'no-referrer' (never send), 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' (default, no HTTPS→HTTP), 'origin' (send origin only), 'origin-when-cross-origin' (full URL same-origin, origin only cross-origin), 'same-origin' (full URL same-origin only), 'strict-origin' (origin only, no HTTPS→HTTP), 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' (recommended), 'unsafe-url' (always full URL). Supported by all modern browsers (Chrome 61+, Firefox 50+, Safari 11.1+, Edge 79+).
DEVELOPER.vulnerability: CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to Unauthorized Actor), CWE-359 (Exposure of Private Personal Information). Information disclosure through Referer header. Attack scenario: (1) User visits https://yourapp.com/search?q=medical+condition, (2) User clicks external link, (3) External site receives Referer: https://yourapp.com/search?q=medical+condition in HTTP header, (4) External site logs and stores sensitive search query. Also exploitable: session tokens in URLs, authentication parameters, internal file paths, user IDs, transaction details. Risk elevated when: sensitive data in URLs, external analytics/advertising, HTTPS→HTTP navigation, user-generated content with external links.

SECURITY_ENGINEER.summary: Missing Referrer-Policy enables information disclosure where sensitive URL parameters leak to third-party sites via HTTP Referer header, creating privacy violations and potential data exposure.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.vulnerability: CWE-200 (Information Exposure), CWE-359 (Privacy Violation). Referer header leakage exposes URL structure and parameters to external parties. Without Referrer-Policy, browsers send full URL in Referer header when: navigating to external sites (same protocol), clicking outbound links, loading external resources (images, scripts from other domains). Information at risk: session tokens, authentication tokens, CSRF tokens, user identifiers, search queries, internal paths, API keys, transaction IDs, personal data in parameters. Particularly dangerous when combined with: insecure session management (tokens in URLs), poor URL design (sensitive data in query strings), mixed content (HTTPS→HTTP navigation).
SECURITY_ENGINEER.attackVector: Passive information gathering attack. Attacker operates external site and monitors incoming Referer headers. Scenario: (1) Victim uses application with sensitive data in URLs, (2) Application has outbound links to attacker-controlled or compromised external site, (3) Victim clicks link, (4) Browser sends full URL in Referer header, (5) Attacker logs and extracts sensitive information from referrer. Also exploitable via: embedded third-party content (ads, analytics), compromised CDNs, malicious browser extensions monitoring network traffic. No user interaction beyond normal browsing required. Completely passive - leaves no traces in victim application logs.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.threatLevel: LOW to MEDIUM - Severity depends on data sensitivity and URL design. Critical if: session tokens in URLs, authentication parameters in URLs, sensitive search queries, healthcare/financial data in parameters. Modern best practice: never put sensitive data in URLs, but Referrer-Policy provides defense-in-depth. Privacy-focused industries (healthcare, legal, finance) should prioritize. Simple fix with no performance impact. Recommended: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' for balance of privacy and functionality.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.mitigationUrgency: Implement within 2-4 weeks as part of security header hardening. Can be bundled with other security headers. Higher priority (1-2 weeks) if: sensitive data in URLs, privacy-sensitive industry, GDPR compliance required, external analytics/advertising integrated. Very low implementation complexity with minimal functional risk. Priority increases to MEDIUM if session tokens or authentication parameters found in URLs (which should be fixed separately as HIGH severity issue).

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.summary: Web servers not configured to send Referrer-Policy header, requiring simple HTTP response header configuration to control referrer information leakage.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.technical: Referrer-Policy header must be added to HTTP responses at web server, reverse proxy, or application layer. Header syntax: Referrer-Policy: <policy-value>. Recommended value: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' (balanced privacy and functionality) or 'same-origin' (stricter, may break external integrations). Typically configured in Nginx, Apache, load balancers, CDN, or application middleware. Simple one-line configuration. Should be applied globally. Consider impact on: analytics platforms (may reduce referrer data), affiliate tracking, external integrations expecting referrer data.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.scope: All web servers serving application traffic: production web servers, load balancers, CDN origin shields, API gateways, reverse proxies. Must be consistent across all environments (dev, staging, production). Applies to all HTTP responses. Consider different policies for: public pages (more permissive), authenticated pages (more restrictive), pages with sensitive data (most restrictive).
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.monitoring: Monitor analytics platforms for referrer data changes after implementation. Verify Referrer-Policy present using security scanners. Use browser DevTools to verify header in responses. Check external integrations still function (affiliate links, analytics). Monitor for broken functionality related to referrer requirements. Include in regular security header audits.

QA_TESTER.summary: Missing Referrer-Policy header prevents validation that sensitive URL information is properly protected from leaking to external sites via HTTP Referer headers.
QA_TESTER.testImplication: Cannot validate referrer privacy controls. Security testing tools (Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP) flag missing Referrer-Policy as low-severity finding. After implementation, must test: (1) Header present on all responses, (2) External links don't leak full URLs inappropriately, (3) Analytics and external integrations still function, (4) Affiliate tracking works if required, (5) No broken functionality from restricted referrer data.
QA_TESTER.riskIfNotFixed: Security audit finding (informational/low severity). Privacy compliance gap. Information disclosure vulnerability. Potential GDPR Article 25 violation (data protection by design). Sensitive URL parameters may leak to third parties. User privacy not adequately protected. Analytics may receive more data than necessary.

django-python.code:
# Django - Add Referrer-Policy via settings
# settings.py

# Method 1: Use Django's built-in SecurityMiddleware
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    # ... other middleware
]

# Set Referrer-Policy (Django 3.0+)
SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin'

# Alternative policies:
# SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'no-referrer'
# SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'same-origin'
# SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'origin'
# SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'origin-when-cross-origin'

# Method 2: Custom middleware for more control
# middleware.py
class ReferrerPolicyMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response
    
    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        
        # Set Referrer-Policy header
        response['Referrer-Policy'] = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin'
        
        return response

# Add to MIDDLEWARE in settings.py:
# MIDDLEWARE = [
#     'your_app.middleware.ReferrerPolicyMiddleware',
#     # ...
# ]

# Method 3: Route-specific policies using decorators
from django.utils.decorators import decorator_from_middleware

def referrer_policy(policy):
    """Decorator to set custom Referrer-Policy for specific views"""
    def decorator(view_func):
        def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
            response = view_func(request, *args, **kwargs)
            response['Referrer-Policy'] = policy
            return response
        return wrapper
    return decorator

# Usage:
@referrer_policy('no-referrer')
def sensitive_view(request):
    return HttpResponse('Sensitive content with no referrer')

@referrer_policy('origin-when-cross-origin')
def public_view(request):
    return HttpResponse('Public content with origin referrer')

# Method 4: Using django-csp package (optional)
# Install: pip install django-csp
# MIDDLEWARE = [
#     'csp.middleware.CSPMiddleware',
#     # ...
# ]
# Note: django-csp focuses on CSP, use SecurityMiddleware for Referrer-Policy

generic.code:
# Generic Referrer-Policy Implementation Guidelines

## Header Syntax

Referrer-Policy: <policy-directive>

## Policy Directives (Most to Least Restrictive)

### 1. no-referrer
- Never send Referer header
- Maximum privacy, may break some functionality
- Use for: Highly sensitive applications

Referrer-Policy: no-referrer

### 2. same-origin
- Send full URL for same-origin requests only
- No referrer for cross-origin requests
- Use for: Applications requiring strong privacy

Referrer-Policy: same-origin

### 3. strict-origin
- Send origin only, never on HTTPS→HTTP
- No path or query parameters sent
- Use for: Good privacy with some functionality

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin

### 4. strict-origin-when-cross-origin (RECOMMENDED)
- Full URL for same-origin
- Origin only for cross-origin
- No referrer on HTTPS→HTTP
- Use for: Balanced privacy and functionality (RECOMMENDED)

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

### 5. origin-when-cross-origin
- Full URL for same-origin
- Origin only for cross-origin
- Use for: Moderate privacy, good functionality

Referrer-Policy: origin-when-cross-origin

### 6. origin
- Always send origin only
- Never send path or query parameters
- Use for: Basic privacy protection

Referrer-Policy: origin

### 7. no-referrer-when-downgrade (Browser Default)
- Full URL for same-protocol
- No referrer on HTTPS→HTTP
- Default browser behavior (don't use explicitly)

Referrer-Policy: no-referrer-when-downgrade

### 8. unsafe-url (NOT RECOMMENDED)
- Always send full URL
- Even on HTTPS→HTTP
- Never use - completely defeats privacy

Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url  # ❌ NEVER USE

## Policy Selection Guide

### Choose 'no-referrer' if:
- ✅ Maximum privacy required
- ✅ Sensitive data in URLs
- ✅ Healthcare, legal, or financial application
- ❌ May break: Analytics, affiliate links, external integrations

### Choose 'same-origin' if:
- ✅ Strong privacy needed
- ✅ Only internal analytics matter
- ❌ May break: External analytics, affiliate tracking

### Choose 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' if: (RECOMMENDED)
- ✅ Balanced privacy and functionality
- ✅ Works with most analytics
- ✅ Protects sensitive URL parameters
- ✅ Best practice for most applications

### Choose 'origin-when-cross-origin' if:
- ✅ Need maximum compatibility
- ✅ External integrations require origin
- ⚠️ Less privacy than strict-origin

## Multiple Policies (Fallback)

# Browsers use first supported policy
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, strict-origin-when-cross-origin

## Implementation Checklist

✅ Choose appropriate policy for application sensitivity
✅ Apply globally to all responses
✅ Test external integrations still work
✅ Verify analytics platforms receive necessary data
✅ Check affiliate links function correctly
✅ Never put sensitive data in URLs (separate issue)
✅ Combine with other security headers
✅ Document policy choice for team

# Generic Referrer-Policy Testing ## Browser DevTools Testing 1. Open browser DevTools (F12) 2. Go to Network tab 3. Navigate to your site 4. Click on any request 5. Go to Headers section 6. Look for Referrer-Policy in Response Headers 7. Verify policy value is appropriate ## Command-Line Testing # Check if Referrer-Policy header is present curl -I https://your-domain.com | grep -i referrer-policy # Expected output examples: Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Referrer-Policy: no-referrer Referrer-Policy: same-origin # Test multiple pages for path in / /search /api/data; do echo "Testing $path:" curl -I https://your-domain.com$path | grep -i referrer-policy done ## Referrer Leakage Test 1. Create test page with external link: Referrer Test

Test Page

URL: https://your-domain.com/search?q=sensitive+data

Click to test referrer 2. Navigate to test page 3. Click external link 4. Check what Referer header was sent 5. With 'no-referrer': No Referer header 6. With 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin': Referer: https://your-domain.com 7. With 'unsafe-url': Referer: https://your-domain.com/search?q=sensitive+data ## Online Testing Tools 1. Security Headers Scanner https://securityheaders.com/ - Enter your domain - Verify Referrer-Policy present and appropriate 2. Mozilla Observatory https://observatory.mozilla.org/ - Comprehensive security scan - Checks Referrer-Policy 3. Referrer Test Tool https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2018/01/understanding-referrer-policy/ - Test actual referrer behavior ## Automated Testing Script #!/bin/bash # test-referrer-policy.sh URL="$1" if [ -z "$URL" ]; then echo "Usage: $0 " exit 1 fi echo "Testing Referrer-Policy for: $URL" RP=$(curl -s -I "$URL" | grep -i "^referrer-policy:" | cut -d: -f2 | tr -d '\r\n ') if [ -z "$RP" ]; then echo "❌ Referrer-Policy header is MISSING" exit 1 else echo "✅ Referrer-Policy: $RP" case "$RP" in "no-referrer") echo "✅ Maximum privacy (may affect analytics)" ;; "same-origin") echo "✅ Strong privacy" ;; "strict-origin-when-cross-origin") echo "✅ Recommended balanced policy" ;; "strict-origin") echo "✅ Good privacy" ;; "origin-when-cross-origin") echo "âš ï¸ Moderate privacy" ;; "origin") echo "âš ï¸ Basic privacy" ;; "no-referrer-when-downgrade") echo "âš ï¸ Browser default (consider stricter)" ;; "unsafe-url") echo "❌ UNSAFE - leaks full URL always" ;; *) echo "âš ï¸ Unknown policy: $RP" ;; esac fi

apache.config:
# Apache - Add Referrer-Policy header
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/your-site.conf or .htaccess

<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName your-domain.com
    
    # Enable mod_headers
    # a2enmod headers
    
    # Recommended: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
    Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    
    # Alternative policies:
    # Header always set Referrer-Policy "no-referrer"
    # Header always set Referrer-Policy "same-origin"
    # Header always set Referrer-Policy "origin"
    
    # Other security headers
    Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
    Header always set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
    
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html
    
    <Directory /var/www/html>
        Options -Indexes +FollowSymLinks
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
    
    # Optional: Different policy for specific directories
    <Directory /var/www/html/public>
        Header always set Referrer-Policy "origin-when-cross-origin"
    </Directory>
    
    <Directory /var/www/html/sensitive>
        Header always set Referrer-Policy "no-referrer"
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>

# .htaccess alternative
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
</IfModule>

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.rollbackPlan:
1. Keep backup of configuration files
2. Document current header configuration
3. If Referrer-Policy breaks functionality (analytics, affiliates), temporarily remove or adjust policy
4. For Nginx: Comment out header line, test with 'nginx -t', reload
5. For Apache: Comment out header line, test with 'apachectl configtest', reload
6. For AWS CloudFront: Modify Response Headers Policy to remove or change Referrer-Policy
7. Identify what broke (analytics, affiliate tracking, external integration)
8. Choose less restrictive policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin → origin-when-cross-origin → origin
9. Re-deploy with adjusted policy
10. Monitor analytics and integrations for 24-48 hours

manualTests.name: Verify Referrer-Policy Header Present

manualTests.name: Test External Link Referrer Behavior
steps: 1. Navigate to page with external links
manualTests.expected: Referrer behavior matches configured policy. Sensitive URL parameters (query strings) not leaked to external sites based on policy.

manualTests.name: Test Analytics and Tracking
steps: 3. Filter for analytics requests (Google Analytics, etc.)
5. Check analytics dashboard for data collection
6. Verify referrer data collected as expected
manualTests.expected: Analytics and tracking platforms continue to function. May have reduced referrer data with stricter policies (expected). Core tracking metrics still collected.

manualTests.name: Test External Integrations
manualTests.expected: All external integrations function correctly. OAuth/SSO flows complete successfully. Payment processing works. Social sharing functions. No Referrer-Policy related errors.
